entry.evidence: it remains unknown what drove this rapid ice-margin retreat during the Early Holocene

steps.action: Pose the question of what drove rapid Early Holocene ice-margin retreat across the marine-terminating KNS forefield, which geologic data alone cannot constrain.
steps.quote: it remains unknown what drove this rapid ice-margin retreat during the Early Holocene

steps.action: Frame two rival drivers: atmospheric forcing acting through surface mass balance, and marine forcing acting through calving and ocean-induced melt.
steps.quote: specifically address how Holocene ice retreat across the KNS forefield was influenced by marine and atmospheric forcings

steps.action: Take the published radiocarbon and 10Be chronology of rapid, synchronous Early Holocene deglaciation of the landscape and fjords as the benchmark.
steps.quote: Collectively, the radiocarbon and 10 Be ages suggest rapid and synchronous deglaciation of both the landscape and fjord systems

steps.action: Build a regional ISSM higher-order thermomechanical model on an anisotropic mesh (1 km in fjords, 15 km elsewhere) with inverted basal friction, enthalpy thermodynamics, level-set front tracking and von Mises stress calving, following the authors' earlier setups.
steps.quote: the horizontal mesh resolution varies from 1 km in fjords and areas of high bedrock relief to 15 km where the bedrock relief is low

steps.action: Design a factorial experiment: high and low temperature and precipitation end members from the Badgeley et al. (2020) reanalysis, fed to a PDD surface mass balance, each run with calving on and calving off (Table 1).
steps.quote: We perform four transient model simulations using four combinations of possible climate scenarios shown in Table 1.

steps.action: Spin up under 12.4 ka climate and run eight transient simulations from 12.4 ka to 2013 CE, starting with the ice margin at the present-day coastline.
steps.quote: Our transient simulations begin 12 400 years ago with the ice margin residing along the present-day coastline for all experiments

steps.action: Map simulated deglaciation ages (youngest ice-free age) and compare them with 10Be and radiocarbon ages; terrestrial surfaces deglaciate up to millennia before the fjords.
steps.quote: To compare against the geologic constraints, we determine when in time portions of our model domain become ice free

steps.action: Exclude calving as a control on the timing of terrestrial deglaciation: calving-on and calving-off runs give similar terrestrial ages, while precipitation shifts them by up to 500-1000 years.
steps.quote: there is little difference between the age of deglaciation on terrestrial surfaces for simulations that allow

steps.action: Plot simulated deglaciation age against elevation and match the geologic absence of an elevation dependence; note that every run ends with present-day ice too far west.
steps.quote: In general, our simulations agree with the geologic data, indicating that there was no elevational dependence on the age of deglaciation

steps.action: Compute Holocene ice-volume trajectories per scenario: runs with calving lose more mass, and the timing of the minimum differs between temperature scenarios.
steps.quote: Broadly, scenarios that allow calving undergo greater ice mass loss than those simulations for which calving is not allowed

steps.action: Compare simulated mass minima and minimum extents with relative sea-level and lake-sediment constraints on a modest mid-to-late Holocene minimum.
steps.quote: Relying on these geologic constraints, we can crudely assess the temporal and spatial patterns of the simulated ice mass and minimum extent.

steps.action: Reject both low-temperature forcing scenarios, whose continued Holocene mass loss conflicts with the geological and relative sea-level records.
steps.quote: Both low-temperature scenarios are inconsistent with the geological record as both show continued ice mass loss through the Holocene.

steps.action: Diagnose 12-10 ka elevation changes and velocity differences: calving accelerates outlets by more than 200 m/yr, propagating thinning inland and reducing interior thickening.
steps.quote: Calving at the ice front leads to increases in ice velocity within outlets across the model domain

steps.action: Compare simulated Early Holocene interior thickening with ice-core thickening of 30-70 m: calving-on runs (<120 m) fit better than calving-off runs (>200 m).
steps.quote: our simulations that allow calving display inland thickening ( < 120 m) over the time interval 12–10 ka that is more consistent with thickening

steps.action: Rerun two scenarios with a 1 MPa grounded-ice stress threshold and with a 120 m/yr sub-shelf melt rate; ice volume is unchanged or barely changed.
steps.quote: adjusting the stress threshold from 600 kPa to 1 MPa has no effect on the evolution of the simulated ice volume

steps.action: Set the precipitation modulation of retreat beside Briner et al. (2020), Downs et al. (2020) and proxy snowfall records, and the terminus attribution beside historical flowband modelling of KNS (Lea et al. 2014).
steps.quote: The pace and magnitude of ice retreat is shown to be modulated depending on precipitation similar to the findings of Briner et al. (2020)

steps.action: Exclude oceanic melting as the primary driver of the longer-term Holocene terminus position.
steps.quote: the longer-term Holocene ice terminus position was also primarily driven by atmospheric warming and not through oceanic melting

steps.action: Defend the omitted auxiliaries: argue that ignoring frontal undercutting is offset by a low stress threshold, and that omitting GIA and relative sea-level change matters little, rather than revising the claim.
steps.quote: we cautiously assume that implementation of undercutting would have a negligible effect on the calving rates

steps.action: Keep the claim that surface mass balance governs terrestrial ice-margin migration while calving-driven discharge governs the rate and magnitude of mass loss, acknowledging an unquantified present-day misfit.
steps.quote: These results confirm that over paleoclimate timescales, while the SMB may dictate large-scale ice-margin migration as captured in geologic observations, ice discharge

steps.quote: We chose this value as it is close to (or within a range of) melt rate values derived for contemporary floating ice shelves

steps.quote: In order to justify and give confidence to our model domain choice, we have added text as follows

steps.action: Narrow the claim that other models' inboard retreat is too extreme so that it refers to the magnitude (20-40 km) of retreat, after RC1 judged it overstated.
steps.quote: we are indeed referring to the ‘scale’ of inland ice margin retreat relative to present day ice margin

steps.action: Decline RC2's request to quantify the percentage contributions of surface mass balance and calving, because the two are dynamically coupled.

steps.action: In response to RC2 on Holocene sea surface temperature, add limitation text on missing subsurface ocean forcing and future PICOP work; no new runs.
steps.quote: Because of these limitation in data, we did not include variation in ocean temperature, and discuss this in Section 5.3

steps.action: Answer RC2's question about the 9.3 and 8.2 ka readvances in the rebuttal only, pointing to pauses in the ice-volume curves not shown in the paper's plots.
steps.quote: Thus, the simulations do show a response to these events, and the ice margin (not shown in the paper plots) does stabilize

steps.action: Decline RC2's suggestion to remove Table 1 (and the opening conclusions paragraph).
steps.quote: We prefer to leave this in as a reminder for the set of experiments needed

No; the drivers are not constrained by geologic data alone and must be simulated

end.claim: Holocene ice-margin retreat across terrestrial parts of the KNS forefield was driven by surface mass balance under Early Holocene warming and was insensitive to fjord calving, whereas calving-driven discharge strongly controlled regional ice mass loss and interior thinning.

decisive_move.sentence: Running each climate end member with calving on and with calving off, then comparing the simulated terrestrial deglaciation ages and ice volumes, is what separates the SMB and calving controls; without these paired runs neither half of the claim exists.

gates.evidence: The paired calving-on/off and climate end-member simulations were designed for the stated question (§3.4 ¶1), but the geologic benchmark data were collected in earlier work (§2 ¶1). The claim could have failed: low-temperature scenarios were rejected (§4.2 ¶5) and calving-on and calving-off runs might have differed on terrestrial ages (§4.1 ¶3). However, model-data fit is judged qualitatively with no misfit metric, and all runs end with present-day ice too extensive (§4.1 ¶6, §6 ¶3). Nothing was fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: von Mises stress criterion used for the calving rate
laboratory tensile-strength measurements of ice (Petrovic 2003, J. Mater. Sci.) bounding σmax
level-set method for tracking the ice front
Courant–Friedrichs–Lewy criterion for the adaptive time step
finite-element discretization with quadratic vertical elements

novelty_claims.quote: it remains unknown what drove this rapid ice-margin retreat during the Early Holocene

limits: The paper shows no quantitative model-data misfit metric; agreement is judged by eye from maps and scatter plots (Figs. 5, 6). No full uncertainty analysis was run, because of computational cost (§4.4 ¶1). Only two parameter variations were made, on two of the eight scenarios. All simulations end with present-day ice too extensive, and the cause is left unquantified (§6 ¶3). The relative contributions of SMB and calving are not partitioned, and the referee's request to do so was declined (AC2-S p.1). Sub-claims and their statuses: calving controls mass loss and interior thinning, best_explanation (model-internal, checked only against ice-core thickening at other sites, §4.3 ¶2); ocean melt played a minor role, best_explanation resting on two sensitivity runs and the omission of undercutting (§4.4 ¶1, §5.3 ¶1); the timing of the Holocene minimum is captured by no simulation, so no conclusion (§4.2 ¶5). Internal inconsistencies: the Figure 12 caption mentions a 6 kPa gray line while the text uses 600 kPa, and §5.3 ¶2 cites Fig. 11 for the sensitivity tests that Fig. 12 shows. Inference: the model setup and boundary conditions are inherited from the authors' earlier work (Briner et al. 2020; Cuzzone et al. 2019), so some design forks predate this paper and are not documented here. Purely stylistic review changes (results text moved to the discussion, colour map, typos) are not coded as steps. Several sentences in the published text (on domain, GIA, the 40 m/yr melt rate, SST) were added at review, as the review record shows, but are coded as author steps in the final_paper sequence per the codebook.

disagreements.target: Ice sheet models simulating 20–40 km of retreat inboard of the present margin (Tarasov and Peltier, 2002; Lecavalier et al., [...]
disagreements.support: Relative sea-level and lake-sediment constraints point to a modest, late Holocene minimum; the authors offer no new data of their own, and the wording was narrowed at review to the magnitude of retreat.
disagreements.quote: the magnitude of large-scale ice-margin retreat inboard of the present-day extent as simulated by some ice sheet models in this sector

disagreements.target: The authors' earlier modelling without ice–ocean interactions (Briner et al., 2020)
disagreements.support: Calving-on runs show substantially greater mass loss and better agreement with ice-core thickening, while terrestrial retreat timing is unchanged.
disagreements.quote: While our past ice flow modeling efforts excluded ice–ocean interactions (Briner et al., 2020)

disagreements.target: Common practice of coarse-resolution (10 km or greater) paleo-ice-flow models
disagreements.support: In the high-resolution runs, fjord calving changes discharge, velocity and interior thinning, which coarse grids cannot resolve.
disagreements.quote: paleo-ice-flow models that do not sufficiently resolve fjord geometry may not capture dynamic processes
